summary:
South Australia stands under the national framework: the federal Sex Discrimination Act has treated gender identity as a protected ground since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that the protection extends to trans women as women, awarding damages against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member. The precedent binds service providers nationally, including in South Australia.

State law supplies a parallel remedy. The Equal Opportunity Act 1984 was amended in 2016 to protect gender identity and sexual orientation, so discrimination on that ground is actionable under South Australian statute as well as federal statute.

Identity documents are the clearest visitor-facing advantage. Since 23 May 2017, under the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration (Gender Identity) Amendment Act 2016 (royal assent 15 December 2016), a South Australian can change the sex descriptor on a birth certificate with appropriate clinical treatment, with no sex-reassignment surgery required and no forced divorce if married. Non-binary and 'indeterminate' sex descriptors are also available on state birth certificates. With the ACT, South Australia was one of the first two Australian jurisdictions to allow the sex recorded on a birth certificate to be changed without sex-reassignment surgery.

Hate-crime sentencing laws explicitly covering sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex characteristics passed and were implemented in November 2021, giving trans visitors protection at sentencing that some other Australian states lack.

Relationship recognition is settled: registered domestic relationships date from 1 August 2017, same-sex couples could adopt from 17 February 2017, and same-sex marriage has been legal since December 2017 under the federal Act, with the 2017 postal survey returning a 62.5% 'Yes' result in South Australia.

Criminal-law history runs in a protective direction. South Australia was the first Australian jurisdiction to decriminalise male homosexual activity, the law commencing 2 October 1975, and it was the last to abolish the gay-panic defence, doing so on 1 December 2020 with effect from 1 April 2021. The Conversion Practices Prohibition Act 2024 passed in October 2024 and is in legal effect from 1 April 2025.

Historical convictions are handled by a distinctive scheme: South Australia is the only Australian jurisdiction whose approach to historical gay convictions is 'spent' rather than expunged, under the Spent Convictions (Decriminalised Offences) Amendment Act 2013, in force 22 December 2013.
tangentialFactors:
Australia's vilification coverage is uneven across states: South Australia, Tasmania and Queensland cover gender identity alongside sexual orientation, while New South Wales, the ACT and Victoria cover only sexual orientation, and the Northern Territory and Western Australia cover neither. Federal hate-crime legislation passed in February 2025 (Act 1 of 2025, effective immediately) explicitly covers sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status, with penalties of up to seven years' imprisonment.

Queensland strengthened discrimination and vilification protections for gender-diverse people in April 2024, and New South Wales passed the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024. The underlying Queensland Human Rights Commission announcement is no longer reachable, and the NSW Parliament bill document would not load, so both rest on the record held here rather than on a live page.

No Australian law confines bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, and no border friction has been reported for trans travellers. Federal law has recognised same-sex couples as de facto partners since 2009, and overseas same-sex marriages are recognised automatically.

Care access for trans minors has tightened nationally since November 2017, when a transgender child could access puberty blockers and hormone treatment without court approval where child, parents and doctors agree, with surgery generally unavailable until 18. In January 2025 the Queensland government paused new prescriptions of puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for under-18s in public health services, exempting existing patients; the Queensland Supreme Court ruled the directive unlawful on 27 October 2025, and a new ministerial directive reinstated substantially the same restrictions on 28 October 2025 pending reviews, with a legal challenge filed in December 2025. A New South Wales independent review released in September 2024 found puberty blockers safe, effective and reversible while calling for more long-term research.

outOfScopeNotes:
The Queensland Human Rights Commission news item on better discrimination protections for gender-diverse people returned HTTP 403 and could not be retrieved; the claim about Queensland's April 2024 reform rests on the record held here rather than a live page. The NSW Parliament bill document for the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024 would not load, so that claim is likewise unverified against a live source.

No source in this inventory addresses South Australian rules on prison placement for transgender detainees, airport or border screening that could expose gender history, or availability of gender-affirming care within South Australian public health services; those questions remain unresolved here.
